title: How Buyers Can Approach Repair Requests After a Home Inspection
content_html:
Once the home inspection is complete, most California buyers reach a pivotal moment in the transaction: deciding what, if anything, to ask the seller to address before closing. The inspection report can run many pages and cover everything from a cracked outlet cover to signs of roof wear, and it's easy to feel overwhelmed trying to figure out what actually matters. This article walks through how buyers typically approach that decision and the negotiation that often follows.

Start by Separating Findings Into Categories

Inspection reports tend to mix minor cosmetic notes with items that affect safety, structural integrity, or major systems. Before drafting any request, it helps to sort findings into rough categories:

  • Safety issues — things like exposed wiring, missing smoke detectors, or a malfunctioning water heater strap.
  • Major systems and structure — roofing, foundation, HVAC, plumbing, and electrical panel concerns that could be costly to fix.
  • Deferred maintenance — items that reflect normal wear, like a worn deck sealant or an aging garbage disposal.
  • Cosmetic or minor — scuffed paint, a loose cabinet hinge, or a cracked bathroom tile.

Buyers generally focus repair requests on the first two categories. Asking for every minor item can come across as excessive and may reduce the seller's willingness to negotiate on the things that genuinely matter.

Understand What the Purchase Agreement Allows

In a typical California purchase agreement, the right to request repairs or credits connects to contingencies the buyer has in place — most often the inspection contingency. If you're unsure how your specific contingencies work or when they expire, it's worth reviewing how contingencies function in a California purchase agreement before drafting a request, since the timeline for submitting one is usually tied to a specific contingency period rather than being open-ended.

It's also worth remembering that the inspection itself is just one piece of what a buyer learns about a property's condition. Reviewing the inspection report alongside the seller's required disclosures can reveal whether an issue noted by the inspector was already something the seller was aware of and disclosed, or whether it's new information. It's worth getting a refresher on what sellers are required to disclose in California before you finalize any request.

Decide Between a Repair Request and a Credit Request

Buyers generally have a few ways to address inspection findings:

  • Ask the seller to complete repairs before closing, using licensed contractors.
  • Ask for a credit toward closing costs or a price reduction so the buyer can handle repairs after closing, on their own schedule and with contractors of their choosing.
  • Ask for a combination — critical safety items repaired by the seller, with a credit for everything else.

Many buyers prefer the credit route for anything beyond urgent safety concerns. It avoids disputes over whether a seller's repair was done to an acceptable standard, and it gives the buyer control over who does the work. On the other hand, for something like a safety hazard that needs to be resolved before move-in, having the seller handle it directly — and provide proof of completion — can make more sense.

Keep Requests Reasonable and Specific

A repair request letter (often prepared by your agent) works best when it references specific items from the inspection report rather than asking in general terms for "all items to be fixed." Vague requests are harder for a seller to respond to and can slow down negotiation. It also helps to prioritize: lead with the items that carry real cost or safety implications, and be prepared for the seller to decline some of the smaller asks.

Sellers are not obligated to agree to any repair request. They can accept it, reject it, or counter with a partial repair or credit. This is a negotiation, not a demand, and going in with that framing tends to produce a smoother outcome for both sides.

Consider the Bigger Picture Before Walking Away

If a seller won't budge on a significant item, buyers still relying on an active inspection contingency generally have the option to cancel the transaction and have their deposit returned, subject to the terms of their specific agreement. Before taking that step, it's worth weighing the issue against the rest of the transaction: Is this a dealbreaker, or something that could reasonably be handled after closing with a contractor of your choosing? A second inspection or a contractor estimate can sometimes clarify whether a finding is as serious as it first appears.

New Construction Has Different Rules

If you're buying new construction rather than a resale home, repair requests after inspection work differently — new homes are covered by California's statutory framework for construction defects rather than a typical resale negotiation. It's worth asking your agent how that process differs before you waive any inspection rights on a new-construction purchase.

Document Everything

Whatever is agreed upon — repairs, credits, or a combination — should be documented in writing as an amendment to the purchase agreement, not left as a verbal understanding. If the seller agrees to complete repairs, buyers often ask for receipts or invoices from licensed contractors as proof of completion, and some buyers choose to do a pre-closing walkthrough specifically to confirm the agreed work was done.

Working With Your Agent Through the Process

Because repair negotiations happen on a timeline tied to contingency deadlines, it helps to have an agent who can move quickly — getting contractor opinions, drafting the request, and communicating with the listing agent without losing days along the way. If you're earlier in the process and want to understand how inspections fit into the overall purchase timeline, it helps to review what to expect before you even get to the repair-request stage.
